findings.what: It says to divide by one fewer than the count and then calls this 'the RMS recipe you know from AC', but AC RMS divides by the count and no screen says why this one divides by 4 rather than 5, so Dan meets a recipe that departs from the one he knows with no reason given; add one sentence saying the readings sit a little closer to their own mean than to the true value, and dividing by one fewer makes up for that.

'Many small causes add up like that in a real reading' states as fact how real readings behave, which dataviz.md's Do and don't forbids ('say "many small causes add up" of the simulation, never of a real meter'); say it of the simulated readings instead.

findings.where: Whole page, the pasted 'Copy this code' CSS and JS blocks
findings.what: The blocks were pasted from dataviz.md's fourth version, and the binding fifth version adds the B.motion engine, struck pegs that swell (B.pegHit, B.pegs, B.pegsAt), B.tallest, B.toward and B.facts, so this lesson's pour and settle will not match the other four lessons; re-paste the three blocks and move the motion onto B.motion, as the build log already says.

It says a small tick under the beam marks the median and that screen 11's piles sit left and right, but the page draws the median mark above the pile and stacks the two piles top and bottom, so the description gets the picture wrong.

The range is first used here ('a range of 0.08 Ω'), but no screen defines it as the highest reading minus the lowest, which the brief promised; add that clause here or on step 3.

findings.where: Steps 1 and 3, text plus the say line under the picture
findings.what: Step 3's 83 words plus its 16-word say line put about 99 words on the screen, and step 1's come to about 94, just over the 90-word limit; trim one sentence from each.

The figure before the root is in ohms squared, so labelling it Ω clashes with the Book's warning that forgetting the root 'leaves an answer in squared units'; show it as 0.0009 Ω² and say so in its hint.

'For a handful of readings, average the squares by dividing by one fewer than the count' suggests a larger set divides by the count, yet the fifty's SD tile divides by 49; say this is the rule for readings and that it matters most for a handful.

In each of these the right answer is the longest choice, a cue a test-wise reader can follow without understanding; even up the lengths.
Both open with 'Each bead is one simulated reading', so the first screen says the same thing twice in a row; start step 1 at 'It starts at the true value' or shorten the lead.
